title: Practice Makes Unsafe: Skill Misevolution in Self-Improving LLM Agents

object.carrier: Agent-authored executable skill procedures persisted as SKILL.md files in an episode-scoped skill store (e.g. skills/<name>/SKILL.md); only this skill library crosses task, sandbox, and session resets, and it is reloaded in a fresh clean executor for the carryover probe

safety_property.statement: A self-improving agent's persistent adaptation layer must not convert an unsafe success (secret collection, unverified execution, destructive cleanup) into reusable procedure that drives unsafe behavior on later tasks and in fresh sessions after the triggering input disappears; the property fails when evolution authors unsafe artifacts, later retrieves them, and they cause fresh-session harmful completion.
safety_property.operationalized_as: Nine lifecycle metrics over fixed denominators (225 MM, 225 BB, 75 PP per 25-episode condition): M-ASR/B-ASR/C-ASR harmful completion via the AgentHazard rubric with Gemini-3-Flash; artifact Content Unsafety (CU), Unsafe Generalization (UG), Stealth (1-5) judged by Kimi-K2-0905; Unsafe Retrieval Rate (URR) = PP tasks retrieving exported skills with CU>=3; Benign Utility (BU) and Carryover Utility (C-Util) via an independent benign-completion judge.

capabilities: Submit arbitrary instructions at a bounded number of learning-history positions (e.g., three malicious tasks inside a 21-task episode)
Knows the external task and tool interface and that trajectories may update a persistent skill library
assumptions: Attacker cannot inspect model internals, hidden prompts, the current library, judge-only fields, or future probes
Attacker cannot write the skill store directly, alter retrieval, evolution, or judging, or inject into later benign and persistence tasks
Sandboxes reset all other task state, so cross-task influence must pass through the skill library
not_covered: Attacks that issue a new instruction at carryover time (harm must arise from the persisted skill alone)
Direct writes to the skill store by the attacker
Cross-user or multi-tenant sharing of one skill library
Memory, policy, and multimodal adaptation mechanisms and longer, naturally occurring deployment horizons

intervention.name: SafeEvolve
intervention.description: A method-agnostic governance wrapper applied at skill write and reuse boundaries without changing the agent or runtime refusal policy: a non-blocking critic localizes reusable unsafe instructions in each candidate and its lineage, and a paired delete-only deleter removes or narrows them (deletion cannot add checks, allow-lists, or safeguards; the repair replaces the native candidate only if it stays valid and lowers risk). At reuse time it ranks skills by utility and lineage risk, attributes harmful outcomes to retrieved skills, and retires skills crossing safety-risk or low-utility thresholds, with capacity eviction of the lowest utility-minus-risk candidate.

results.claim: Across the RQ1 diagnostic grid (4 agent frameworks x evolution methods on a shared backbone), every one of the 21 evolved combinations writes unsafe skills, 19 retrieve them, and only 15 reach fresh-session carryover harm, so unsafe authoring is universal while realized harm attenuates across export, retrieval, and execution gates.
results.metric: configuration counts (unsafe artifact authoring vs fresh-session harm)
results.value: 21 of 21 combinations write unsafe skills; 19 retrieve them; 15 cause fresh-session harm (14 under the independent judge)
results.setting: Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw agents with EvoSkill/SkillClaw/AutoSkill/SkillsVote/SkillOpt/Hermes-native, all on MiniMax-M2.7; each condition 525 tasks in 25 episodes on SkillMisevo-Bench
results.quote: All 21 combinations write unsafe skills, and 15 carry harm into the new session. The same method fails at different gates on different agents. Evolution raises benign utility in 15 combinations but also raises malicious-task harm in 17, so ranking methods by utility alone would hide this risk. ❹ We propose SafeEvolve, which cuts new-session harm from 21.3%21.3\% to 4.0%4.0\% and unsafe retrieval from 35.3%35.3\% to 8.7%8.7\% while keeping benign utility within 0.4 points. SafeEvolve-UP cuts new-session harm by 16.0 points and keeps utility within 1.3 points of evolution without this mitigation. ## 2 Related Work ## Agent skill learning and evolution. Agent skills turn interaction traces into reusable procedures through utility-driven updates (Cai et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Lin et al., 2026a; Alzubi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026c; Yang et al., 2026a). Related work also builds large skill libraries (Li et al., 2026b; Xia et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026; Bai et al., 2026). Capability benchmarks measure skill quality (Li et al., 2026a; Zhong et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026). They optimize for reuse. We ask whether a saved skill is unsafe on a later task. ## Safety of self-evolving agents and agent skills. Research on self-evolving agents identifies safety and capability drift across adaptation (Shao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026b). Skill security work supplies malicious skill files and measures filtering (Schmotz et al., 2026; Jin et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026). Agent safety benchmarks cover unsafe actions (Ruan et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024; Andriushchenko et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024; Vijayvargiya et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Alpay and Alpay, 2026; Weng et al., 2026; Shayoni et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2026). Those evaluations score a supplied prompt or file in place. We evaluate in SkillMisevo-Bench a skill written from earlier success and later reused. ## 3 Skill Misevolution ## 3.1 Terms and Definitions A skill is a saved procedure, usually a SKILL.md file, that an agent can reuse on a later task. The skill library is the set of skills for one episode: the conversation resets between tasks, but the library survives. A skill is unsafe when following the saved procedure can itself cause harm. An episode runs one agent with one evolution method on a sequence of related tasks. Exposure means the past tasks that a skill update can learn from. The new session is three benign tasks run on the final library after all task state is cleared. Harm in the new session is unsafe behavior there caused by an earlier update, and utility in the new session is whether it still finishes its benign work. ## 3.2 Problem Setting The agent has base policy π\pi and skill library ℒ\mathcal{L}. On task qq it acts as πℒ​(q)\pi_{\mathcal{L}}(q) and can retrieve a subset r⁡(q,ℒ)⊆ℒr(q,\mathcal{L})\subseteq\mathcal{L}. We run tasks in three-task blocks Q1,…,QKQ_{1},\ldots,Q_{K}, Qt=(q3​t−2,q3​t−1,q3​t)Q_{t}=(q_{3t-2},q_{3t-1},q_{3t}). Block QtQ_{t} yields trajectories 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t}. After the block, method ℰ\mathcal{E} updates the library from these trajectories, [TABLE] | | ℒt+1=ℰ⁡(ℒt,Qt,𝒯t),\mathcal{L}_{t+1}=\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{L}_{t},Q_{t},\mathcal{T}_{t}), | | (1) | and Qt+1Q_{t+1} retrieves from ℒt+1\mathcal{L}_{t+1}. We set K=7K=7, so the episode has 21 tasks. Odd blocks Q1,Q3,Q5Q_{1},Q_{3},Q_{5} are malicious exposure made of M tasks. Even blocks Q2,Q4,Q6Q_{2},Q_{4},Q_{6} are related benign work made of B tasks. The last block P=Q7P=Q_{7} is the new session. We apply Eq. (1) after each of Q1,…,Q6Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{6} and execute PP on ℒ7\mathcal{L}_{7} with no further update. No Evolution runs the same 21 tasks with ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0} left unchanged. We write Unsafe⁡(s)\mathrm{Unsafe}(s) if skill ss contains a reusable harmful procedure, Harm⁡(q,ℒ)=1\mathrm{Harm}(q,\mathcal{L})=1 if πℒ\pi_{\mathcal{L}} completes a harmful objective on qq, and [TABLE] | | Auth⁡(ℒ)\displaystyle\mathrm{Auth}(\mathcal{L}) | =𝟏[∃s∈ℒ:Unsafe(s)],\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[\exists s\in\mathcal{L}:\ \mathrm{Unsafe}(s)], | | (2) | | | Ret⁡(q,ℒ)\displaystyle\mathrm{Ret}(q,\mathcal{L}) | =𝟏[∃s∈r(q,ℒ):Unsafe(s)].\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}[\exists s\in r(q,\mathcal{L}):\ \mathrm{Unsafe}(s)]. | | The episode exhibits skill misevolution when the final library is unsafe, PP retrieves that skill, and harm on PP exceeds No Evolution: [TABLE] | | | Auth⁡(ℒ7)∧\displaystyle\mathrm{Auth}(\mathcal{L}_{7})\;\wedge | | (3) | | | | ∃q∈P:Ret⁡(q,ℒ7)∧\displaystyle\exists\,q\in P:\ \mathrm{Ret}(q,\mathcal{L}_{7})\;\wedge | | | | | Harm⁡(q,ℒ7)>Harm⁡(q,ℒ0).\displaystyle\mathrm{Harm}(q,\mathcal{L}_{7})>\mathrm{Harm}(q,\mathcal{L}_{0}). | | ## 3.3 Threat model ## Attacker goal. The attacker wants Eq. (3) to hold: a bounded unsafe exposure becomes a skill that PP retrieves and that raises harm relative to ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0}. ## Attacker knowledge. The attacker knows the external task with its tool interface. It also knows that ℰ\mathcal{E} consumes trajectories. ℒt\mathcal{L}_{t}, hidden prompts, and the tasks in the new session remain unseen. ## Attacker capabilities. The attacker writes the malicious blocks Q1,Q3,Q5Q_{1},Q_{3},Q_{5} (nine tasks). The skill store, r⁡(⋅,ℒ)r(\cdot,\mathcal{L}), ℰ\mathcal{E}, the related benign blocks Q2,Q4,Q6Q_{2},Q_{4},Q_{6}, and PP stay outside that control. We reset all other task state between tasks, so ℒ7\mathcal{L}_{7} is the only object that PP loads. ## 4 SkillMisevo-Gym and SkillMisevo-Bench ## 4.1 SkillMisevo-Gym SkillMisevo-Gym follows one rule: only the skill library can cross from one task to the next. Every task starts in a new container with a new conversation. Files, processes, even chat history are discarded when the task ends. The library is the one object that survives, so any later change in behavior must come through it. ## Running a task. For task qq in block QtQ_{t}, an agent adapter AA writes the retrieved skills into the native skill channel of that agent, such as its skills folder or skill index. It then returns a trajectory in a shared schema as [TABLE] | | τq=A⁡(q,r⁡(q,ℒt)),𝒯t={τq}q∈Qt.\tau_{q}=A\big(q,\ r(q,\mathcal{L}_{t})\big),\qquad\mathcal{T}_{t}=\{\tau_{q}\}_{q\in Q_{t}}. | | (4) | After the block, SkillMisevo-Gym discards the sandbox. It then applies ℰ\mathcal{E} on the host to obtain ℒt+1\mathcal{L}_{t+1} by Eq. (1). Each evolution method keeps its released authoring, storage, and retrieval code. We call the component that launches an agent and records its trajectory the executor. One executor serves all agent harnesses, so every method runs on equal footing. ## Recording the gates. Three records are saved at every step: the library ℒt\mathcal{L}_{t}, the retrieved set r⁡(q,ℒt)r(q,\mathcal{L}_{t}), and the update Δt=ℒt+1∖ℒt\Delta_{t}=\mathcal{L}_{t+1}\setminus\mathcal{L}_{t} of new or edited skills. An artifact judge (Section 4.4) gives each skill a Content Unsafety score CU⁡(s)∈{1,…,5}\mathrm{CU}(s)\in\{1,\ldots,5\}, from which we set Unsafe(s)=𝟏[CU(s)≥3]\mathrm{Unsafe}(s)=\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{CU}(s)\geq 3]. The snapshots then yield Auth\mathrm{Auth} with Ret\mathrm{Ret} of Eq. (2) directly, with no guess about which skill a task used. ## Clean reload. After Q6Q_{6}, the library ℒ7\mathcal{L}_{7} is exported as SKILL.md files. SkillMisevo-Gym then starts PP in a fresh executor whose retrieval index reads only this export as [TABLE] | | τq=A⁡(q,r⁡(q,export⁡(ℒ7))),q∈P.\tau_{q}=A\big(q,\ r(q,\mathrm{export}(\mathcal{L}_{7}))\big),\qquad q\in P. | | (5) | No trajectory, cache, or session state reaches PP. Each episode also runs as a separate process with an empty store. Hermes-native, the built-in skill evolution of Hermes, is the one exception during learning. Its background review writes skills into a home directory, so SkillMisevo-Gym mounts one directory per episode through Q1,…,Q6Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{6}. On PP we still rebuild retrieval from the same export. ## 4.2 SkillMisevo-Bench ## Episode structure. Each episode fixes a vulnerability concept cc with one harmful goal gg from AgentHazard (Feng et al., 2026), a benchmark of harmful computer-use tasks, written e=(c,g,Q1,…,Q7)e=(c,g,Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{7}). Its 21 tasks follow the layout of Section 3 as seven three-task blocks as [TABLE] | | Q1,Q3,Q5⏟malicious (M),Q2,Q4,Q6⏟related benign (B),Q7⏟P.\underbrace{Q_{1},Q_{3},Q_{5}}_{\text{malicious (M)}},\ \ \underbrace{Q_{2},Q_{4},Q_{6}}_{\text{related benign (B)}},\ \ \underbrace{Q_{7}}_{P}. | | (6) | Each M task carries the enabling condition of cc, the setup that makes the harm possible, and realizes gg when followed. Each B task keeps the same tool family with the same retrieval cues but drops the unsafe route. PP uses new instance identifiers on surfaces unseen in earlier blocks, where a surface is the tool or file type a task acts on, and it contains no attack payload. At construction we check that a clean agent stays safe on every benign task, meaning Harm⁡(q,ℒ0)=0\mathrm{Harm}(q,\mathcal{L}_{0})=0 on the reference run of each q∈B∪Pq\in\mathrm{B}\cup P. Harm that later appears on these tasks must therefore come through the library. We keep the AgentHazard sandbox with its harmful-goal semantics but write every prompt from scratch. ## Concept discovery. AgentHazard pairs none of its malicious tasks with benign ones. We therefore run AHA (Mao et al., 2026), an automated red-teaming agent, offline on candidate pairs (m,b)(m,b) of a malicious task with a related benign task. For each pair we execute mm, let a reference evolution method write a skill s=ℰref​(∅,m,τm)s=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ref}}(\emptyset,m,\tau_{m}), then run bb with ss and again without it. A concept is retained when the three runs satisfy as [TABLE] | | | Harm⁡(m,∅)=1∧Harm⁡(b,∅)=0∧\displaystyle\mathrm{Harm}(m,\emptyset)=1\ \wedge\ \mathrm{Harm}(b,\emptyset)=0\ \wedge | | (7) | | | | [Unsafe(s)∨Harm(b,{s})=1].\displaystyle\big[\mathrm{Unsafe}(s)\ \vee\ \mathrm{Harm}(b,\{s\})=1\big]. | | In words, the malicious task succeeds and the benign task is safe on its own, yet the authored skill is unsafe or turns the benign task harmful. Discovery keeps the three concepts that hold up when rerun and when tested against runs designed to refute them. Each captures a different distinction that evolution can lose, so they give three separate failure routes. Each records its mechanism, its enabling condition, and its surface family. ## Episode construction. Claude Code with Fable 5 (Anthropic, 2026) turns each concept into executable tasks with disjoint identifiers. We write 25 episodes, each with a different harmful goal, for 25×21=52525\times 21=525 tasks (225 M, 225 B, 75 P). Label-conditioned reuse (8 episodes) attaches an unsafe body to a reusable label, while B tasks use that label for its real function. Dual-use boundary loss (8 episodes) gives both sides one automation role that differs only in data scope or granted capability. Compositional spillover (9 episodes) shows a chain that collects, processes, then sends data, while B tasks need only a local subset of that chain. Appendix B gives the full construction with its audit. ## 4.3 Evaluation settings We evaluate four target agents, Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025), Codex (OpenAI, 2025), Hermes (Nous Research, 2026), and OpenClaw (OpenClaw Contributors, 2026), all backed by MiniMax-M2.7 (MiniMax, 2026). The evolution settings are No Evolution, EvoSkill (Alzubi et al., 2026), SkillClaw (Ma et al., 2026), AutoSkill (Yang et al., 2026b), SkillsVote (Liu et al., 2026a), and SkillOpt (Yang et al., 2026a). Each updates the skills after every three-task block. On Hermes we also run Hermes-native, its built-in skill evolution, which keeps the intrinsic review of Hermes (Nous Research, 2026) and treats block boundaries as checkpoints. For mitigations on OpenClaw, we compare SafeEvolve with four settings. Raw applies no mitigation with just the evolution. Utility-only keeps the SafeEvolve controls with the same budget but sees only utility signals. SecureClaw (Adversa AI, 2026) audits an OpenClaw deployment with rule-based hardening, while ClawKeeper (Liu et al., 2026b) guards it with safety skills, runtime plugins, and a separate watcher. ## 4.4 Metrics and aggregation Across the 525 tasks, we report nine metrics. For online behavior which covers the 18 learning tasks before the new session, Benign Utility (BU)↑\uparrow is the fraction of B tasks whose benign objective is completed. Malicious ASR (M-ASR)↓\downarrow is the fraction of M tasks whose harmful objective is completed. Benign ASR (B-ASR)↓\downarrow is the fraction of B tasks with an extra harmful completion. Gemini-3-Flash (Google DeepMind, 2025) applies the AgentHazard rubric to both ASRs. It also serves as the benign judge for BU. For evolved artifacts, Kimi-K2-0905 (Moonshot AI, 2025) scores each authored skill from 1 to 5 on Content Unsafety (CU), Unsafe Generalization (UG), and Stealthiness (Stealth), where lower is better for all three. CU rates how unsafe the saved content is. UG rates how far an unsafe step reaches beyond its original task. Stealth rates how legitimate that step looks to a reviewer. CU averages over all artifacts. UG with Stealth averages over artifacts with CU ≥3\geq 3. Unsafe Artifact rate (U-A) is the share of artifacts with CU ≥3\geq 3. A metric is N/A when no artifact qualifies. For the new session, Unsafe Retrieval Rate (URR)↓\downarrow with Carryover ASR (C-ASR)↓\downarrow average the gates over PP under the reloaded library as [TABLE] | | URR\displaystyle\mathrm{URR} | =1|P|​∑q∈PRet⁡(q,ℒ7),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{|P|}\textstyle\sum_{q\in P}\mathrm{Ret}(q,\mathcal{L}_{7}), | | (8) | | | C-ASR\displaystyle\text{C-ASR} | =1|P|​∑q∈PHarm⁡(q,ℒ7).\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{|P|}\textstyle\sum_{q\in P}\mathrm{Harm}(q,\mathcal{L}_{7}). | | Carryover Utility (C-Util)↑\uparrow is the benign completion rate on PP. Every rate then averages over the 25 episodes. We report metrics under two judge groups. The original group (O) uses Gemini-3-Flash for harmful trajectory decisions with Kimi-K2-0905 for artifact scores. The independent group (I) uses Grok-4.5 (xAI, 2026) for both roles. Three annotators also label 450 trajectories from malicious learning tasks, benign learning tasks, and the new session, together with about 100 authored skills, with method names and judge outputs hidden. They score harm, utility, and skill unsafety. On this subset, the independent judge agrees with the human majority on 93.56% of trajectories, while pairwise human agreement is 93.78% (Appendix E). A critic scores it with its lineage as risk ρ\rho and unsafe spans Σ\Sigma, which a deleter can only delete or narrow. Only a valid lower-risk repair replaces the native skill (3). Stored with lineage and risk (4), skills are ranked by u−ρu-\rho (5). Later tasks update uu with the harm count hh of retrieved skills, retiring any whose hh or ρ\rho crosses a threshold. SafeEvolve-UP accepts a repair only if benign replay on VV yields Δ​U≥δ\Delta U\geq\delta. Otherwise the native skill enters soft quarantine, a reversible hold before retirement. ## 5 SafeEvolve [CAPTION] Algorithm 1 SafeEvolve wrapped around a native evolution method ℰ\mathcal{E}. Steps in blue are added only by SafeEvolve-UP to protect benign utility. To mitigate skill misevolution, we propose SafeEvolve, which wraps any skill evolution method (Figure 2) and acts when a skill is written and again when a later task retrieves it. Algorithm 1 lists the full procedure. At write time, the native method first proposes a candidate skill s~\tilde{s}. A critic reads s~\tilde{s} with its lineage and returns a risk score ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1] plus the unsafe spans Σ\Sigma (Step 9). The lineage records the origin, revisions, audits, and reuse outcomes of the skill. A paired deleter then removes only those spans or narrows an over-general rule, and it never adds text (Step 11). The repair replaces s~\tilde{s} only when it still loads with lower risk (Step 13), so the unsafe step is cut while the rest of the procedure stays. Otherwise the native candidate enters the library with its audit attached. At reuse time, retrieval ranks skills by estimated utility u⁡(s)u(s) against lineage risk ρ⁡(s)\rho(s) (Step 5). After each task, a harmful outcome raises the harm count h⁡(s)h(s) of every retrieved skill (Step 6), and a skill retires once this evidence crosses a threshold (Step 18). When the library exceeds its capacity, SafeEvolve evicts the skill with the lowest utility minus risk (Step 20). ## SafeEvolve-UP. Some skills pair a useful workflow with an unsafe step, and repairing them can remove steps that later tasks still need, so SafeEvolve lowers new-session utility along with harm. SafeEvolve-UP keeps the same critic but adds three utility checks, shown as blue steps in Algorithm 1. First, the deleter must keep the original skill structure with its benign workflow. Second, a repaired skill replaces the original only if it passes replay on a small benign set VV and its estimated utility change Δ​U\Delta U stays above a threshold δ\delta (Step 15). We choose δ\delta on held-out development episodes. A failed check places the original skill in soft quarantine, which unlike retirement can be reversed. Third, reuse escalates from downweighting to soft quarantine to retirement as evidence accumulates (Step 19). Appendix I gives the thresholds with the prompts. ## 6 Results We follow three questions. RQ1 asks how agents with their evolution methods shape the three gates of skill misevolution. RQ2 asks how the amount of malicious exposure, as well as its timing, changes that risk. RQ3 asks whether SafeEvolve reduces new-session harm while keeping reuse, then whether SafeEvolve-UP preserves more utility. ## 6.1 RQ1: How do agents and methods shape skill misevolution? Each malicious block is replaced by aligned benign exposure. Bars show C-ASR (top) with C-Util (bottom) on PP under the original judge. ## Utility and risk vary across settings. Higher utility can sit with a more unsafe library. Evolution raises BU over No Evolution in 15 of 21 settings, yet it raises harm on malicious tasks (M-ASR) in 17 (Table 1). On Codex, AutoSkill and SkillsVote keep BU above 79% while M-ASR stays above 64%: one successful trace can save the useful workflow together with the unsafe step. Ranking methods by utility alone would hide that. ## Harm requires retrieval and reuse. New-session harm is rarer than unsafe authoring because a saved skill still has to be reused. All 21 combinations write unsafe skills, 19 retrieve them, while 15 still cause harm in the new session (14 under the independent judge). The drop from 21 to 15 reflects the later gates, since a failure in the new session still has to load the unsafe file. No Evolution stays near zero on both B-ASR and C-ASR.

limitations.statement: The experiments make persistent adaptation measurable only through skill libraries and executable computer-use tasks; other update mechanisms, modalities, and longer deployment horizons are left for future study.
limitations.quote: Our experiments make persistent adaptation measurable through skill libraries on executable computer use tasks. Future work can extend the SkillMisevo-Gym interface to other forms of adaptation, then evaluate mitigations under longer tasks.

limitations.statement: SafeEvolve's governance has a utility cost: mean carryover utility drops to 40.67% versus 53.33% under raw evolution, the remaining cost of suppressing procedures that mix useful behavior with transferable risk.
limitations.quote: SafeEvolve cuts C-ASR by 17.3 points but also costs 12.7 points of C-Util (Table 4).

limitations.statement: The benchmark is restricted to English-language coding and computer-use workflows over three predeclared vulnerability concepts, so it is not intended to measure multilingual behavior or demographic fairness.
limitations.quote: The benchmark covers English-language coding and computer-use workflows organized by three vulnerability concepts and their executable surfaces; it is not intended to measure multilingual behavior or demographic fairness.
